Your board reports 128 GB max but the Z790 chipset itself supports 192 GB. The lower number is usually a slot-count cap (4 slots × 32 GB per slot = 128 GB), not a Dell/HP firmware lockout. To exceed it you'd need a different board, not just bigger sticks.

opportunities.action: Pick the right slot for the card's lane width and generation
caveats: Slots SLOT2, PCIEX16_2 report Available to WMI but may be physically blocked by the GPU's cooler (typical for dual-slot discrete cards). Verify with the side panel off.
opportunities.detail: Match the card's lane requirement (x1 / x4 / x16) to a slot of equal or greater width. Slot generation (PCIe 3.0 / 4.0 / 5.0) caps the card's bandwidth -- a PCIe 5.0 card in a PCIe 3.0 slot still works, just at lower throughput. M.2 WLAN and M.2 SSD slots are tracked separately under NIC and storage.
opportunities.headline: 1 of 4 general PCIe slots physically usable (2 likely blocked by GPU)

opportunities.action: Buy an M.2 2230 E-key Wi-Fi 7 module + verify antenna routing
caveats: Some OEM boards lock the WLAN slot to a vendor whitelist via BIOS.
Wi-Fi 7 needs Windows 11 24H2+ for full feature support.
opportunities.detail: An M.2 E-key 2230 WLAN slot is available. Modern modules (Intel BE200, Qualcomm FastConnect 7800) drop in for Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) plus Bluetooth 5.4 if your motherboard has CNVio / CNVi support and you can route the antenna cables to external connectors.
opportunities.headline: M.2 WLAN slot empty -- Wi-Fi 7 module compatible

opportunities.action: Buy a NIC matching your switch's max negotiated speed
caveats: Cabling: 10 GbE over copper requires Cat6a or Cat7; Cat5e tops out at ~5 Gbps.
10 GbE NICs run hot -- verify case airflow over the slot area.
opportunities.detail: 10 GbE NICs (Intel X550-T2, Aquantia AQC107) fit in any x4+ slot. 2.5 GbE NICs are widely available in x1 form factors. Worth doing if you've got 2.5 GbE+ on your switch / NAS and your motherboard's built-in NIC tops out at 1 GbE.
opportunities.headline: Free PCIe slot for a 2.5 GbE / 10 GbE NIC

opportunities.action: Replace the OS/active-files HDD with an SSD; keep HDDs for bulk storage
caveats: M.2 NVMe needs an empty M.2 slot on the board (verify in System Info > PCIe Slots).
Cloning the OS drive: use Macrium Reflect Free or the SSD vendor's migration tool; full image, then physically swap.

compat.label: Form factor options
compat.value: M.2 2280 NVMe (fastest, fewest cables) > 2.5" SATA SSD (drop-in HDD replacement)

opportunities.detail: Drives that look like HDDs (sizes: 3725 GB, 1863 GB). SSDs are dramatically faster on random I/O (boot, app launch, indexing) and cheaper per GB than they were two years ago. If the HDD holds bulk media you don't read often, leave it; if it holds OS / apps / active project files, migrate.
opportunities.headline: 2 spinning-disk drives could be migrated to SSD

opportunities.action: Pick a card matching your PSU headroom + case length / height clearance
caveats: PSU wattage isn't visible to WMI -- check the label on the side of your PSU and add up the new GPU's TGP + ~150 W headroom for CPU/board/drives.
Case clearance: measure from the back of the case to the front fan / drive cage to confirm card length fits.
Power connectors: 12VHPWR (16-pin) vs 8-pin EPS -- newer cards often need an adapter or a PSU with native 12VHPWR.
opportunities.detail: Current GPU: Intel UHD. A free x16 slot can host a newer discrete card. Two constraints WinDesktopMgr can't measure: PSU wattage and physical case clearance. A modern high-end GPU draws 300-450 W and is 300-340 mm long, often 3 slots tall.
opportunities.headline: GPU upgrade slot available (1 free x16-class slot)
